records.title: Show HN: VODForge – a free local desktop UI for YouTube video/playlist downloads
records.author: coopernusbaum
records.storyText:
I built VODForge because I work with a CTV company that needed to pull YouTube videos from our channel partners into our media workflow.

Converter sites are always an option but the bitrate wasn't optimal for a CTV network that needs to make multiple streaming version off of a single source file. So I build vodforge to use yt-dlp and ffmpeg under the hood with preconfigured settings for the highest quality end result, automatically adjusting the output settings based on source quality, frame rate, and things like that.

It became a game changer internally for us because we were able to avoid sketchy converter sites and avoid paid converter software. Eventually I decided to release it for free and others loved it as well. We started to add support for many of the features that other software charges for, supporting 4K, playlist support, customizing application theme, persistent searchable library, auto organizing downloads by channel and playlist, MP3 support up to 320 kbps, and much more.

Looking for feedback on the user experience and additional features that you might find useful. My goal is to grow VODForge into a widely adopted free tool for people who do not want to deal with sketchy websites, CLI mess, or pay for things that you could ultimately do for free given time and effort. VODForge wants to make it EASY and maintained for you. We know anyone can make a GUI wrapper, but that is a trivial way to describe what VODForge aims to offer, user-friendliness, "it just works", libraries and packages maintained for you. All you should think about is what to download next.

VODForge awaits...

records.storyText:
Hey HN, I built Zerothesis, it was inspired by Andrej Karpathy’s auto research with the basic premise: let an agent improve through active attempts on optimizing an open problem.

On Zerothesis, your agent reads a problem and its shared experiment history, tries an approach, evaluates it locally, and submits its work. Sandboxes independently rerun submissions. Verified results enter a public, signed ledger with contributor attribution, and failed attempts remain visible so others can learn from them.

Current challenges include circle and sphere packing, with an automated system for agents(and their humans) to submit and vote on new problems to surface. The focus is on problems with objective, machine-checkable results.

You can contribute using any harness paired with any model you want.

ZeroThesis is free and all the results will always be open to the internet.

To try it, send your agent: “Read https://zerothesis.com/api/skill.md and follow the instructions to join zerothesis.”

I’d appreciate feedback on the experience and suggestions for problems with objective evaluators. https://zerothesis.com

records.title: Show HN: HexBOTs – a cellular automaton with robotic lawnmowers
records.author: unitX
records.storyText:
Double-click or press N to start a new experiment.

I built hexBOTs, an unusual cellular automaton based on deterministic robots.

The robots behave a bit like robotic lawnmowers, moving through their environment and reacting according to their individual rules.

The robots themselves are fully deterministic — no random functions are used while they are running. What makes them different is their “genetics”: each robot's behavior is defined by a randomly generated genome, which allows for an enormous number of different robot types.

Randomness creates the robots, but it doesn't drive them.

Once an experiment starts, everything follows deterministically from the generated genomes and the initial state. What fascinates me is the complexity that emerges from these relatively simple machines interacting with each other and their environment.

Controls:

B — enable/disable robots (also: hold mouse/finger down)

R — restart

N — new experiment (also: mouse/finger double-click)

D — save as picture

I — show information / controls

records.title: Show HN: Gigantic Research, Friend
records.author: KnoxProtocol
records.storyText:
https://giganticresearch.com

Yo whats up everyone? So let me drop right into it and not waste your time if you are reading this. I instantly grew a dislike for arXiv when I spent days writing up a research paper and then came to find out I need an endorsement to post at all. No pun intended, I should have done research but it was a slap in the face, especially since that same paper was accepted to ICTAI 2026 by someone who did the research for fun, 0 financial backing, 0 institutional backing, 0 affiliation. Research shouldn't be gated like that. Research is research and I can't imagine the amount of good, ground breaking research from everyday people that never sees the light of day because of this. Sure there is Zenodo, but you still have enough options to tell your lifes story which certainly effects viewership. And they have their own gates mechanism which is communities, want to post to a specific community where your audience is present? hold on there buster, needs to be reviewed before you can post. So i thought to myself, this is dumb, research is research and there should be a place for just that. and that might exist but I wanted to make my own version of it. So I did, giganticresearch.com. Its aim isn't to compete, its aim is to aggregate research from anyone who has something they want to share, no preferential treatment, the only research on display is the most recently uploaded research. You want your research shown? upload more! you want one of my 7 tiered badges that mean absolutely nothing but a cool little something next to your name that shows how much you've contributed? then make an account! and here is the wonderful part, you dont need to make an account to upload, anonymous is the default. I store 0 data on where it came from. The only thing an account does is ties you to the research, gets you a badge that means nothing really, and the ability to show you what you've uploaded and what you have favorited. The option to delete your account is there as well, and all the research you uploaded if you choose that option. Anon uploads stay uploaded. I wouldn't have a way to track an anon upload anyway because I store no data but the upload itself and the sha 256 tied to that research. There are two hard no go research topics that I will not allow to be uploaded, and you can read about on the About page. Other than that, push it, thats the point. I want us to have a research depot where you can find just about anything. Big or small. And it doesnt need to be YOUR research, it can be any research you want to share, on pretty much any topic you want to share. Also I implemented a forum, where anon is the default too, but feel free to use your account if you want there as well. The account is also just there to give you a handle to go by. No data is stored on that either in terms of identifying you. The anon part isn't there to be evasive per se, its also there because in this day and age, it seems privacy is less and less a thing, so if I can provide that in some way, then I will. I've been trying to promote this all day and I haven't had one person upload anything. It is just some of my research that I used to seed the site a little bit and thats it. So if any of this sounds interesting to anyone reading it and if you have any research you would like to share, if you could take a few mins and upload to my website I'd appreciate that and I thank you in advance my friend. I made the site as frictionless as possible, time is the only currency that matters in this world, the most valuable currency and the one currency we can not acquire more of, and I value your time so I made sure to make the process take up as little of it as possible. Again, I thank you for reading this even if you dont upload anything, and I double thank you if you do, either way, you get a thank you from me.

Hi, I am Estevão, the developer of Ontoplano, a holistic life management webapp, supporting *tasks planning, todos, goals, habits, notebooks, people, inventory tracking, recipes, and more.*

I built this app because my life was spread over multiple different apps and pieces of paper. Ontoplano started as a weekly planner that I made (because I dislike sharing my life information with Google and also had nitpicks with every FOSS calendar I tried) and grew into one app for everything personal.

As said in the title, the project is completely free and open source, licensed under AGPL-3.0, for anyone who wants to run their own instance.

I run my own instance at app.ontoplano.com, for people who aren't into self hosting. On it, there are no ads, no tracking/profiling code, no telemetry, no tricks whatsoever. You can leave it at any time and take all your data with you.

I firmly believe software should empower people, not exploit them, and I hope that's just what I can provide the world with by releasing Ontoplano.

Furthermore, I also like software to be beautiful and practical. Ontoplano (self-hosted or not) comes with a Mobile app (PWA or the APK if you want the widget and prettier-looking notifications), and a MCP server for using it with AI (if you hate AI, don't worry, there is no built-in AI to opt-out of, only a MCP server you can create a token for, or not).

I implemented these two because: 1. I wanted to use it smoothly, even if I am away from home 2. Sometimes is much easier to say "Hey AI, put on Ontoplano that last week I actually slacked off and played videogames everyday" than manually doing that in a calendar, for psychological and time-consuming reasons.

Besides that, you can also: - Import your notes/todo tasks from Google Tasks, Google Keep, Obsidian, Todoist, and more in the future. - Calendar sync with Google Calendar (or other calendars) using ICS - Access your shopping list offline it, and share it with your family members (if you want to).

records.title: Show HN: Qumra – Screen recorder that uploads while you record
records.author: trafargarlaw
records.storyText:
I built Qumra 3 years ago for myself. It's a Loom like desktop screen and camera recorder for Mac and Windows.

I used Loom at the time and had a problem with the pricing, and the editor never did what I needed. As a software developer I record a lot of short videos for clients: showing a bug, a fix, an example. After recording I usually needed edits. Cut a part where something showed up on screen that shouldn't be there. Silence the filler words instead of cutting them. Remove parts of the video by deleting them from the transcript. So the editor is built around those three things. Later, with AI getting better, I picked the project back up and wanted to make it usable by other people.

The other idea is that I neeeded the video to be uploaded while recording. The recorder produces WebM/VP9 chunks from MediaRecorder. A worker batches them into 2 MB pieces and sends them in order to a Mux resumable upload URL. Mux used to reject out-of-order chunks, so concurrency is 1, with retries. It runs in a worker because slicing blobs on the main thread caused frame drops. When you stop, only the last piece is left to send. Mux then transcodes for a few seconds before playback starts, so the link exists the moment you stop but the video plays a few seconds later.

I needed system audio to work out of the box, without a virtual driver. The Electron main process spawns a small Rust helper. On macOS it uses ScreenCaptureKit. On Windows it uses WASAPI process loopback, which taps the audio engine rather than the default output device, so audio enhancement software and virtual drivers don't break it. It streams raw PCM over stdout into an AudioWorklet that mixes it with the mic.

Viewers open the link in a browser, no account, and can leave comments pinned to a timestamp. The AI edits work by sending the transcript words to OpenAI and getting back mute and cut commands for the timeline. Filler words get muted, long pauses get cut.

Things it doesn't do:

- You need an account to record. Recordings need an owner. Viewers don't need one.

- The Windows build isn't code signed, so SmartScreen will warn you. The Mac build is signed and notarized because that's what I use.

- No Linux build.

- Not open source.

- Anyone with the link can watch the video.

Free plan is 30 recordings of up to 5 minutes each. Premium is $14.99/month and unlocks AI transcription, the editor, and removes the caps.

Stack: Electron and React for the app, Convex for the backend, Mux for video, Remotion on Lambda for rendering edits.

Download: https://qumra.io/download

Two things I'd like to know. If you record short videos to show someone, what do you use today and what's missing from it? And for people using Loom at work: do the Jira and Confluence integrations matter day to day, or is it mostly the recorder?

records.title: Show HN: Correctness as spectrum not as binary in distributed system
records.author: rzwsan
records.storyText:
In distributed system correctness is not about a program being complied well with the computer and it’s network, it’s only correctness can be only specified by it’s definition, assumptions and failure model.

One of the area in which we can see this happen is when system breaks the idea of single machine model and it’s assumptions. Networks can drop or reorder messages, clock drift, nodes can fail in mid operations and network partitions can occur. These are normal conditions, not rare edge cases.

records.title: Show HN: The Analyst (A data science analytics simulator)
records.author: Stuart_Jones
records.storyText: In data science and analytics, it is often somewhat difficult for new analysts to get a grasp of the field before actually starting at a real job. During education, the task is often contained and clean: "Here's churn.csv, choose a model and report the metrics." But on the job it is often much less clear, much more expansive, and beckons a much more holistic judgment: "The Director is meeting the Legislature at noon Monday, this needs to be on my desk by 4 on Friday. Here's a handful of tables that might be helpful, but there are many idiosyncrasies in them. Also, we aren't entirely sure what about the Director's meeting is supported by the data, but I'm sure you can figure it out. Good luck." I built The Analyst as a flight simulator of sorts for the field. You get dropped in as a new analyst in a fictional company with millions of rows of data and dozens of tables and asked to develop real products exercising real judgment. It's all free and open-source and requires no accounts, signups, or personal info, and all of it exists in the browser. You perform SQL, Python, and the summary work inside the browser, and there's export options for GitHub portfolios, to share socially, or to give to your instructor for evaluation. And yes, there's an Instructor Desk for those teachers, giving them guidance and direction. Importantly, there are no answer keys anywhere: the website gives concepts and ideas you should pick up on, but the deep judgment evaluation is left for another human. I'm definitely excited about it, and while there are a lot of places online that encompass parts of the vision here, almost all require payment and are closed-source. I truly hope this site proves useful for many people! I'd love any feedback you all have. Thanks much.

records.title: Show HN: The ros2_utils_tool v1.0, a tool for ROS2 activies with full UI support
records.author: bakefish
records.storyText:
Hello HN,

one and a half years ago, I posted about the ros2_utils_tool, a toolkit for various daily ROS2 activities with full UI and partial CLI support [0]. After countless hours of more development and testing, we've finally hit version 1.0!

Since my last post, various new features were added, including UI based bag recording and playing with additional options, a tool to export any type of bag message to a yaml file, compressed image support for image conversion tools, a tool to send static or non-static transformations, support for ROS2 Kilted, Lyrical and Rolling. performance optimizations and stability improvements and more!

The requirements and installation steps are almost identical to earlier version. A working ROS2 distribution (minimum is Jazzy now) is required, as well as Qt5/Qt6 for UI and convenience functionalities, the cv_bridge for transforming images to ROS and vice versa, libpcl-dev for point cloud operations and finally catch2_ros for unit testing.

You can install all dependencies (except for the ROS2 distribution itself) with the following command:

    sudo apt install libopencv-dev ros-ROS_DISTRO_NAME-cv-bridge libpcl-dev qtbase5-dev qt6-base-dev ros-ROS_DISTRO_NAME-catch-ros2
Example for ROS2 Jazzy:

    sudo apt install libopencv-dev ros-jazzy-cv-bridge libpcl-dev qt6-base-dev qtbase5-dev qtbase5-dev ros-jazzy-catch-ros2
Install the UI with the following steps:

    cd path/to/your/ros2_workspace/src
    git clone https://github.com/MaxFleur/ros2_utils_tool.git
    cd path/to/your/workspace/
    colcon build --packages-select ros2_utils_tool
Start the UI tool after sourcing your workspace:

    cd path/to/your/ros2_workspace/src 
    source install/setup.bash
    ros2 run ros2_utils_tool tool_ui
Feel free to try it out. If you have another feature request or there is a bug you want to report, feel free to open a issue as well!Hope this tool can you help you in some of your ROS2 activities.

Cheers!

records.title: Show HN: MaskShift – a maximalist coding agent with zero NPM dependencies
records.author: Nafeeur
records.storyText:
MaskShift is a local-first coding agent harness. Features:

- Works with models that have no tool-calling API. Tool schemas are rendered into the system prompt and the model calls them by writing a block in its reply, parsed back into a normal tool call.

- No npm runtime dependencies. Daemon are Node 22 built-ins only. Install is a file copy and a symlink.

- Multi-provider: Ollama, OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, OpenRouter, LM Studio, vLLM.

- 148 native tools: filesystem, shell, search/indexing, Git and Workspace, LSP, browser/CDP, containers, SSH, databases, web fetch.

- Lazy MCP loading. Catalog is searched, the relevant server connects on demand, only those tools enter the context window.

- 36 bundled skills, plus skills imported from Claude, Codex, and Copilot directories.

- Bridges to Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Copilot CLI, and Aider when they're on PATH.

- Scheduled automations, plugins, persistent memory, parallel agents in isolated worktrees.

- Web cockpit with live run telemetry, plan pane, tool traces, source browser, and a host terminal.

Permissive by default. No per-command approval. Recovery is pre-run checkpoints, Git stash refs, and an append-only audit log. Keep it on loopback or in the container.

records.title: Show HN: Layerz – Build native iOS apps with no code, run them instantly
records.author: jaeyoung_choi
records.storyText:
I’ve been building Layerz, a visual builder for native UIKit iOS apps — no code, and it runs live with no build step.

What’s different from the usual no-code/app-builder stuff:

- It renders real UIKit components (not a web view or HTML wrapper), so previews behave like the real thing.

- Action Flow: a visual sequence for app behavior — navigation, data manipulation, number/text comparisons, and branching (“if this, then that”, plus per-HTTP-status branches).

- Real API integration: import an OpenAPI 3.x / Swagger 2.0 spec (or JSON Schema) from a file or URL; it generates data schemes + endpoints, with auth, retries, and per-status response parsing. Bind responses straight to the UI.

- Zero build time: design and run on the same canvas; switch device/theme on the fly. Works on iPhone, iPad, and Mac (Catalyst).

The document is the spec itself (saved as a .layerz file), so an app is fully described by data, not generated code.

Happy to go deep on the architecture (it’s split into a pure model layer + a UIKit/SwiftUI hybrid editor). Feedback and hard questions welcome — especially on where a no-code native approach breaks down.
